Not an answer but I'm also in the same boat as you. I'm 16, and most people view 16 year old computer nerds as hipsters who make websites (sad but true). But I actually have a passion for programming, but I have no idea of how to set myself apart from others my age apart from making projects. I've been told by professional programmers about how good I am at programming, but I sometimes don't believe them and I don't see a way for me to get into the industry with how oversaturated the market is. It's a sad situation right now, the computer science field is.
It's not the fault of CS programs. The glut of "required" bullcrap gen ed classes leave no time for a more diverse comp sci curricula.

This is certainly part of it. While a well-rounded education is important, that should be on high schools to impart. University is for specialization. However even if they put more emphasis on CS classes, it won't change too much in the end. Right now there is a false equivalence going on of CS Degree == Programmer. A CS degree should be teaching computer science. It should NOT be a programming training school. There are systems out there specifically to teach 'real world' programming, which is these days usually web dev. A CS grad who has the necessary natural talent for programming will have a much higher ceiling potential and be able to adapt to changing tech demands better. However if a person isn't cut out for true CS, then they will get far more out of a practical coding curriculum.

I've met, hired, and fired many programmers through my career, and there is one thing that stands out about all the best ones: They made big personal life sacrifices to get to the level they are at. Their CS friends went out partying Friday night, they stayed in their dorm learning to use sockets (and not because it was a class assignment). I'm not saying the sacrifice is worth it, its different for everyone, but most people don't realize just how much time and effort it takes to get to a 'highly skilled' programming level, let alone a truly 'elite' level.

I concur as to both the time requirements to become an effective programmer being quite high, and also CS teaching more than just programming. Object Oriented Design, Algorithm Efficiency, and Database Structures are common CS courses that aren't "How to program", but rather /how you should think about computers."

Though I have to disagree about whether CS should teach programming. I see it as similar to how an Accounting degree teaches both the mechanical task of bookkeeping, general ledger entries, etc, and also how to apply GAAP to determine how to handle situations where you have multiple valid choices, but need to choose the ideal one for your circumstances using your judgement.

As to WebDevs...they make me eyebulge, because most of the ones I encounter know the mechanical side of writing scripts and some code, but most direly need the balance of Comp Sci's normative training in algorithm efficiency so they would understand the difference between "working" and "working well".

Oh I didn't mean to imply that CS shouldn't teach programming. I am more upset with my managing peers in the industry who think a kid right out of CS should be a productive programmer in business. Just like an accountant right out of school might be able to manage a mom and pop's restaurants books but likely not a Fortune 500 company's, a CS grad should have been taught enough programming to support learning and exploring the science of computers, but likely not enough to build your next-gen 'scalable but cheap' startup idea.

In traditional engineering disciplines for example, say chemical engineering, it would be rare for a firm hiring a fresh grad to expect high level productivity. Usually they are brought in an paired with an experienced team who teaches them how to apply that university knowledge to their business domain.

You're spot on. Fresh Comp Sci grads know just enough to be dangerous. Coding's learning curve is so steep that a fresh grad is basically the equivalent of someone with their first full drivers license. They need a lot more training and experience to drive semis or race cars.

I agree and disagree. I'm not a fast programmer, I don't do it enough anymore to remember all the syntax. But, I've never written the same piece of code twice. Why would I? Also if somebody else has written it, why reinvent the wheel? Having said that, what I think is a problem is if they don't understand what the code they copied does. That's a very big problem.

Also if somebody else has written it, why reinvent the wheel?

If we don't periodically reinvent the wheel, then wheel technology never improves. Sometimes you must reinvent the wheel to discover new ways to use wheels or better methods to make them. The same goes for code. If we did not reinvent our code again and again, then we'd still be programming in Cobol and Fortran on punch cards. Do you really want to ride around on stone wheels attached to your car?

There are a wide array of reasons to invent the wheel. The most practical is simply that most non-industrial open source software is poorly written. As there's been a push to make open source trendy I expect the quality is going to even further deteriorate. I've ended up rewriting the vast majority of open source stuff I tried to integrate into my projects simply because it'd take less time to write it from scratch than to wrap my head entirely around their implementation and then debug that - and my implementation often ends up being more performant on top of that. In the process I can also migrate the component to my projects native datatypes instead of having to convert them somewhere along the line.

I also think this is a reason so much modern software is so buggy. When projects are relying on 100 different projects nobody on the team working on the primary project actually wrote, there is going to be "unexpected behavior" and the behavior may become all but impossible to track down once the project reaches a certain scale. Add in stuff like asynchronous and parallel execution and it becomes even riskier to integrate third party projects simply because debugging becomes that much harder and even perfectly functional code in one context can suddenly start deadlocking or generally bugging out in another.
